LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson takes the deck’s loudest sound and teaches it in three sizes: big roar, middle roar, whisper-roar — volume control smuggled into pure fun.

What is this?

A lion is the big wild cat with a mane that says ROAR — the sound every toddler already owns from books, songs and the back garden.

What does it mean?

Playing with volume teaches that the voice has a dial. Loud and soft are opposite words learned in the body, and opposites are the backbone of early thinking.

What does the child need to know?

Roaring can tip into over-excited fast. The built-in answer is whisper lions: the same game at a volume the house can survive, and toddlers find whisper-roars just as funny.

Why this matters

The lion is the card a wiggly toddler seeks out on a grey afternoon — it is a permitted explosion, and permitted explosions end naps on time.

What it teaches

Volume modulation, emotional release through pretend play, and the mane as a first stand-out feature — spotting details is where observation begins.

Words to learn

lionroarloudwhispermanewild

Say this to your child

“"A lion! The big cat says ROAR. Can you roar? Giant roar… now a small roar… and the tiniest whisper-roar — shh, the lion is sleeping. Big hair, big voice!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say lion, then ROAR — the biggest roar the living room allows.
  2. Roar in three sizes together: giant, middle, mouse-sized. Hold up hands to show which size comes next.
  3. Hunt lions in books and toy boxes; every found lion gets the size of roar your toddler chooses.
  4. When the roar comes out as a scream, bless it once — then offer the whisper version: "now roar like a tiny lion." The switch resets the game.
  5. Give roars their slots this week: big roar after nap, whisper-roar before bed, and a middle one at bathtime.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows a lion saying roar. Find the lion, find the roar word, then ask where the lion’s big hair is — the mane is the detail this card exists to name.

Ask your child

"Where is the lion?" "What does the lion say?" "Can you do the giant roar?" "Can you whisper-roar so baby doesn’t wake?"

What your child can say or do

A full-body "ROAR!" with the chest pushed out is standard delivery. Whisper-roars arrive with a finger on the lips — that gesture alone is worth the whole lesson.

Out in the real world

Lions live in story books, zoo visits and the rug at home. Books are the daily stage: one lion page, one roar, one size chosen by the toddler — the deck’s fastest routine.

Try it together

Sleeping lions, toddler edition: everyone roars, then flops down as a sleeping lion, then wakes with one giant ROAR and flops again. It burns the last energy of the day and ends in a lie-down by design.

Understanding check

Ask what the lion says. A roar in any size passes. Then ask for the tiny lion — if the volume drops on request, the voice-dial has been installed and the lesson is complete.

Parent tips

Own the reset: when roaring tips past fun, go whisper without scolding — the game continues, the volume teaches. Zoo lions mostly sleep, so manage that expectation with one honest sentence before you go.

Staying safe

Zoo lions are behind glass and barriers for good reasons — hold your toddler at the rail, and remind them gently that a real roar means the lion is telling everyone this is its home.

This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).
